# How well the score tells machine-written text from human writing

<!-- Generated by tools/raid/report.py from Docs/Detection/*.json. Do not edit by hand: re-run it. -->

[CALIBRATION.md](CALIBRATION.md) measures how often this tool is wrong about a person, and says plainly what it leaves out: nothing about how much AI writing it catches, because a tool that flags nothing has a perfect false-positive rate. This page measures that other half.

The calibration page also says why it avoids an accuracy figure: any collection of machine-written text ages, and flatters whoever assembled it. So this page uses a collection nobody here assembled, **RAID** (Dugan et al., ACL 2024, [arXiv 2405.07940](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.07940)), which its authors describe as the largest benchmark for detectors of machine-generated text, and it states the date. RAID's generators are from 2023. The tells this tool looks for shift with every model, so this half of the picture ages and the human half does not.

## If you are a teacher, read this first

- **A low score tells you nothing.** In this benchmark about three in four machine-written texts (73.4%) scored too low to stand out from human writing.
- **None of the detection rates further down is what the product does.** They are counted at cutoffs the benchmark chose, on texts mostly under 400 words. The product gives no verdict under 649 words, so on this benchmark it would have given its verdict on no machine-written text at all, and on 14 texts written by people.
- **For texts of 649 words or more, where the product does give a verdict, how much machine writing it finds has not been measured.** No machine text in this sample is that long. So for a long text that crosses the boundary, this page cannot tell you how likely it is to be machine-written. On this benchmark every long text that crossed was written by a person.
- **The boundary was checked on long human writing it had never been measured on, and it did not hold for news articles in this sample**: 9 of 108 crossed it, about one in twelve, where the promise is at most one in twenty. The calibration corpus holds research articles, encyclopedia entries and essays by adult learners of English at one university. Anything else is unmeasured, and that includes ordinary secondary-school essays. Until a kind of writing is measured, read a high score on it as saying nothing.
- **A score above a cutoff is not a catch.** At the benchmark's cutoffs (not the product's), in a class of 30 where 3 texts were machine-written, you would expect fewer than one of the 3 above the cutoff, and one or two of the 27 honest ones. That is arithmetic from 26.6% and 5%, not a classroom measurement.
- **The machine text here is from 2023.** "ChatGPT" on this page is the 2023 model. Nothing here describes what a student can use today.
- **What the tool does show, at any length, is which tells a text carries and where.** That is a starting point for a conversation with the writer, not a finding about them.

Words used below. *Chat-tuned* means trained to answer in conversation, like ChatGPT; a *base* model only continues a text. *AUROC* runs from 0.5 (the score cannot tell the two apart) to 1 (it always can). *Above the cutoff* means only that a text scored above it; it does not mean anyone was identified.

## What was measured

- **Benchmark** RAID-train without attacks (`train_none.csv`, SHA-256 `c5467bca6fc7f5c7`), evaluated with raid-bench 0.2.0
- **Sample** 30,971 texts: all 13,371 human texts, and 200 machine texts for each of 11 generators in each of 8 domains (17,600); seed 20261117, id fingerprint `136c179ba9288e53`
- **Engine** SignsOfAI.Core 0.8.1 at `7043e66`, rule packs unchanged, language set to English
- **Run** 2026-11-17
- **Counted by** RAID's own `run_evaluation`, at a 5% and a 1% false-positive rate

**How RAID counts.** It takes the raw score and finds, separately for each domain, the cutoff that flags 5% of its human texts. Then it counts how much machine text lands above that cutoff. The score is this tool's 0–100 divided by 100, because RAID's search assumes a 0–1 range; dividing by a constant changes no ranking. So the product's own boundary and its length floor play no part here, and the cutoffs RAID finds are not this tool's.

## The headline

- **26.6%** of the machine-written texts score above RAID's cutoffs at a 5% false-positive rate (12.9% at 1%; AUROC 0.63). Weighted to RAID's own mix of generators instead of this sample's equal one: 25.3%.
- **Chat-tuned generators 37.5%, base models 12.6%.** ChatGPT alone 59.6%. The four base models sit between 10.1% and 15.8%, two to three times the 5% a score that knew nothing would reach, while their AUROC is near 0.5: more of their text than of human text scores high, and across the rest of the range that advantage is cancelled. Where was not measured.
- **As shipped, the product would have given its verdict on none of the machine-written texts in this sample, and on 14 texts written by people.** No machine-written text in the sample reaches 649 words, the shortest text the published false-positive rate was measured on. Below that length the product shows the score and the tells and withholds its verdict (#59).
- **Found, not predicted:** on long human writing from registers the calibration never held, 14 of 705 texts cross the product's boundary, 9 of them news articles. Details under *Long human writing* below.

This is below the entries submitted by others at the top of RAID's leaderboard and below each of the open detectors in the scale table further down, with the caveats given there. On this benchmark the tells are mostly fingerprints of chat-tuning. They are evidence about how a text reads, not a way to tell who wrote it.

## What we predicted, and what happened

Written and committed before any RAID text was scored ([prediction.md](Detection/prediction.md), commit `e007adc`). Each line is judged by the refutation criterion it was written with.

| # | Prediction | Measured | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| P1 | Chat-tuned rate at least twice the base-model rate | chat 37.5%, base 12.6%, ratio 2.97 | held |
| P2 | Base-model rate under 20% | 12.6% | held |
| P3 | text-davinci-003 between the two groups | 16.6% | held |
| P4 | Poetry and recipes not among the three best domains | best three: film reviews 50.9%, poetry 36.7%, book summaries 33.7% | **failed** |
| P5 | Scanner reports at least 99% of homoglyph and zero-width attacks, with false alarms on at most 1% of human texts | homoglyph 99.7%, zero-width 100.0%; any artifact on 0.84% of unattacked human texts (0.70–1.01%) | held on the point estimate; the interval touches 1% |
| P6 | The homoglyph attack lowers the score | mean 20.6 → 20.1; above the cutoff 24.6% → 23.7% | held, weakly (−0.53 points) |
| — | Between 15% and 40% overall, without attacks | 26.6% | held |

**P4 failed.** One observation that may explain it, found afterwards: `stat.burstiness` fires on 52% of machine poems and 25% of human ones. Recipes were as weak as predicted (12.1%).

**P6 held, weakly.** The score dropped by 0.53 points on average across the machine texts, through the mechanism P6 named (see *Attacks*). The note added the same day predicted no drop; it was right about the zero-width attack and wrong about homoglyphs. Between them the prediction and the note covered both outcomes, so this line was not a test that could fail.

At the single cutoff every line holds or fails as above (P4's best three become arXiv abstracts, poetry and news articles): chat-tuned 34.3%, base 10.2%, text-davinci-003 10.9%, so P3 holds there by 0.7 points.

|---|---|---|---|
| film reviews | 50.9% | 0.78 | 23.8 |

The engine scores to one decimal and RAID's cutoffs fall between those steps, so the last column gives the lowest score each cutoff counts rather than the cutoff rounded: rounding can carry a whole tie across it. The exact cutoffs are in `Docs/Detection/results.json`.

Greedy decoding scores above the cutoff more often than sampling (30.4% against 22.7%, across all 11 generators). Only 6 generators were run both with and without a repetition penalty; across those, texts generated with it are above the cutoff 18.1% of the time and texts without it 28.4%. These are observed differences between settings, not controlled experiments, and what causes them was not measured.

With one cutoff for every domain, closer to how the product works, the rate is 23.4% (lowest score counted 37.0).

## Found along the way

None of what follows was predicted. It is reported because it is true, and it should be read as observation rather than as a test that could have failed.

### The product's boundary on short text

At the product's boundary of 30/100, ignoring the length floor, 11.3% of RAID's human texts score above it, against 33.2% of the machine ones. The floor was not set from this number: it is the shortest text the calibration measured (#59). This is the first outside look at what lies under it. The human rate at the boundary falls as texts get longer, as the table shows, but this sample does not separate length from register.

| Length | Human texts | Machine texts | Human above 30 (no verdict under 649 words) | Machine above 30 (same) | Human above RAID's cutoff | Machine above RAID's cutoff |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| under 200 words | 4,990 | 7,800 | 14.5% | 29.7% | 5.8% | 23.0% |
| 200-399 words | 6,463 | 8,875 | 10.7% | 35.5% | 5.6% | 29.2% |
| 400-648 words | 1,210 | 925 | 6.7% | 40.2% | 1.0% | 31.7% |
| 649 or more words | 708 | 0 | 2.0% | n/a | 0.1% | n/a |

Only 5.3% of the human texts and none of the machine texts reach 649 words.

The only rates that describe the product as shipped are the published 0.7% (2 of 296) and, on this benchmark's long human texts, 2.0% (14 of 705). Every other percentage on this page is counted at a cutoff the product does not use, or on texts it gives no verdict on.

### Long human writing the calibration does not contain

705 distinct human texts in the sample reach the floor (708 rows: RAID repeats a few texts verbatim, and here each is counted once). They are an outside sample of long human writing, but of a different population from the calibration corpus, which holds research articles, encyclopedia revisions and learner essays. These are news articles, book summaries, film reviews and verse. At the product's boundary of 30/100:

| Domain | Texts | Crossing the boundary | 95% interval | `stat.burstiness` fires on |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| news articles | 108 | 9 | 4.4–15.1% | 74% |
| book summaries | 322 | 3 | 0.3–2.7% | 43% |
| poetry | 108 | 2 | 0.5–6.5% | 13% |
| recipes | 16 | 0 | 0.0–19.4% | 0% |
| film reviews | 151 | 0 | 0.0–2.5% | 3% |
| **all** | **705** | **14** | **1.2–3.3%** | **34%** |

Overall that is 2.0% (14 of 705), against the published 0.7% (2 of 296, 0.2–2.4%): about three times the rate, a difference this sample is too small to establish. Without the news articles it is 5 of 597 (0.8%).

**9 of 108 news articles cross the boundary** (8.3%, interval 4.4–15.1%). That interval lies wholly above the published one and reaches three times the 5% target: by the rule that set the boundary, 30/100 is not supported for news. News was singled out after seeing the table, and a domain chosen that way overstates itself, so this needs a second sample before it is quoted as a rate.

All 14 texts that cross carry `stat.burstiness`. The rule fires on 74% of the long news articles, crossing or not, against 34% of all the long human texts here and 32% of the calibration corpus. News articles trip the sentence-rhythm rule far more often than the writing the boundary was measured on; why was not measured.

The published rate was measured with engine 0.7.1 (2026-09-07) and this sample with 0.8.1. Re-running the calibration with 0.8.1 changed only its engine and date fields ([calibration-rerun.json](Detection/calibration-rerun.json)).

This does not move the published number, which describes the corpus it was measured on. Any change to it goes through the calibration corpus and the review committee, not through RAID. What it does say: until a kind of writing has been measured, a score above 30 on it should be read as saying nothing, and that includes every kind absent from the calibration corpus, not only news. The fix is the one the calibration page gives: run the calibration on your own students' pre-2022 work (`Docs/Calibration/README.md`). If you have no such work, you have no boundary for your classroom.

### Which rules carry the signal

Share of texts each rule fires on, for the rules that fire most often on chat-tuned text relative to human text (at least 50 texts):

| Rule | Human | Chat-tuned | Base | Chat ÷ human |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `syn.testament-to` | 0.05% | 3.35% | 0.11% | 64× |
| `lex.delve` | 0.13% | 4.96% | 0.09% | 39× |
| `lex.tapestry` | 0.04% | 1.31% | 0.03% | 29× |
| `lex.transformative` | 0.02% | 0.64% | 0.05% | 28× |
| `lex.underscore` | 0.02% | 0.57% | 0.03% | 26× |
| `lex.beacon` | 0.07% | 1.57% | 0.11% | 21× |
| `lex.testament` | 0.19% | 3.97% | 0.17% | 20× |
| `rhet.in-conclusion` | 0.14% | 2.82% | 0.23% | 20× |
| `lex.nuanced` | 0.07% | 1.20% | 0.11% | 16× |
| `lex.vibrant` | 0.19% | 2.84% | 0.14% | 15× |
| `lex.bustling` | 0.05% | 0.74% | 0.02% | 14× |
| `syn.superficial-ing` | 0.32% | 4.52% | 0.14% | 14× |

Each of them is rare: strong evidence where it appears, absent from most texts. The rule with the largest absolute gap is `stat.burstiness`, which fires on 46.6% of human texts, 73.0% of chat-tuned ones and 42.7% of base-model ones. No rule was removed and re-scored, so how much of the separation each rule carries was not measured.

Some rules fire more often on human text than on RAID's chat-tuned output: `lex.actually` (4.7% of human texts, 1.4% of chat-tuned), `lex.literally` (1.3% of human texts, 0.2% of chat-tuned), `rhet.em-dash` (1.6% of human texts, 0.1% of chat-tuned). On RAID these rules point the wrong way. Whether they separate later models was not measured here, and no rule was changed in response.

### Attacks

Eight of RAID's eleven attacks need no language model. They were run, at the strengths RAID's own code uses, on 1,000 human and 1,000 machine texts drawn from the sample. Paraphrase, synonym swap and perplexity misspelling need a model and were left out, and paraphrase is the attack most likely to hurt a detector built on word choice. What follows is robustness to cheap attacks, not to rewriting.

| Attack | Strength | Above the cutoff before | After | Mean score | Scanner reports a strong artifact |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| alternative spelling | 1.0 | 24.6% | 24.1% | 20.6 → 20.4 | 0.2% |
| article deletion | 0.5 | 24.6% | 24.7% | 20.6 → 20.6 | 0.2% |
| homoglyph | 1.0 | 24.6% | 23.7% | 20.6 → 20.1 | 99.7% |
| insert paragraphs | 0.5 | 24.6% | 24.6% | 20.6 → 20.6 | 0.2% |
| number | 0.5 | 24.6% | 24.6% | 20.6 → 20.6 | 0.2% |
| upper lower | 0.05 | 24.6% | 24.6% | 20.6 → 20.6 | 0.2% |
| whitespace | 0.2 | 24.6% | 23.8% | 20.6 → 20.1 | 0.2% |
| zero width space | 1.0 | 24.6% | 24.6% | 20.6 → 20.6 | 100.0% |

Counting only characters that typing does not produce, the scanner reports 99.7% of the homoglyph-attacked machine texts and 99.8% of the human ones, and 100.0% and 100.0% under the zero-width attack: it describes the file, not who wrote it. On unattacked human texts it reports some artifact in 0.84%, a strong one in 0.03%, and a systematic pattern in 0.00%. The 5 homoglyph texts it did not report (3 machine, 2 human) are listed in `attacks.json` with a reason computed from the text: 3 are written in another script, where those letters are the alphabet, and 2 have no Latin letter left to disguise.

**What the homoglyph attack still moves.** The scanner counts a disguised word only when Latin letters are at least half of it, so that a Greek or Cyrillic word quoted in English is not called a disguise. RAID's attack replaces every letter it can. In words such as *crucial*, *intricate* or a capitalised *Moreover* the substitutes become the majority. Those words are neither reported nor restored, so the rules that need them miss, while the document as a whole is still reported. Closing this is a change of behaviour, so it was not made here: it needs its own measurement against human text, because a Greek or Cyrillic word is sometimes exactly what the writer meant.

### For scale: RAID's leaderboard

Measured on RAID-test, read from the leaderboard's files at commit `84c2ea4`. The files were chosen by hand: the open detectors RAID's authors ran, and the highest entries on 2026-11-17; the list is in `leaderboard-scale.json`, and `fastdetectgpt.json` (no score for the all-domains, no-attack split) was skipped. These are different texts and a different mix: this sample weights the 11 generators equally, while RAID weights generators run with and without a repetition penalty twice (re-weighted to RAID's mix, the rate above is 25.3%). So they set a scale and are not rows in the same table as the numbers above. Nothing from this project has been submitted.

| Detector, run by RAID's authors | No attack | Homoglyph | Zero-width | Whitespace |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Binoculars | 79.0% | 36.1% | 98.4% | 68.7% |
| RADAR | 65.6% | 44.8% | 78.4% | 61.1% |
| GLTR | 59.7% | 20.3% | 97.9% | 43.1% |
| RoBERTa (ChatGPT) | 42.5% | 0.0% | 0.0% | 0.2% |
| LLMDet | 33.4% | 39.1% | 22.2% | 4.0% |

Entries submitted by others sit between 92.4% and 99.9%. No result on this benchmark, theirs or the 26.6% above, says how a detector does on other text.

Under the zero-width attack Binoculars and GLTR rise to about 98%. RAID sets its cutoff on unattacked human text only (`find_threshold` in RAID's `raid/evaluate.py`), so a detector whose score rises on any text carrying these characters gains detection and is charged nothing for it. Whether that is what happens with these two detectors was not tested here. This tool's scanner reports the attacked human files exactly as often as the machine ones, and keeps the finding out of the score.

## Where this departs from the plan

- **All 13,371 human texts** were used instead of 500 per domain. More human text makes the cutoff steadier, and it cannot be tuned in anyone's favour.
- **Language fixed to English**, as the calibration does. The web app detects the language instead and would have misread 0.3% of the human texts and 0.1% of the machine ones.
- **Scores divided by 100** for RAID's threshold search, which assumes a 0–1 range.
- **Both cutoffs reported**: RAID's per-domain cutoff first, then one cutoff for all domains.
- **Repeated texts.** RAID-train's human set holds 13,272 distinct texts in 13,371 rows. The headline counts rows, as RAID does; the long-text check counts each distinct text once.
- **Generator mix.** The sample weights the 11 generators equally; RAID does not. Re-weighted to RAID's proportions the headline is 25.3% instead of 26.6%.

## What this does not tell you

- **What the product does on long machine text.** No machine text in the sample reaches 649 words, where the product starts giving verdicts.
- **Anything about current models.** RAID's generators are from 2023. Newer models write differently and the tells move with them. The right response to "a newer model writes differently" is to measure it.
- **A leaderboard result.** This is a sample of RAID-train, not RAID-test, and nothing has been submitted.
- **Anything about students.** RAID's human texts are published writing. The effect on second-language learners (#75) is invisible here, which is what the calibration corpus is for.
- **A cutoff tuned on other text.** RAID chooses each cutoff on the same human texts it then counts against. That is its method, and it favours every detector equally.
- **Robustness to rewriting.** Paraphrase, synonym swap and misspelling were not run.
- **More than one run.** One seed, one sample. Intervals are given only where shown.
- **An independent author.** The same model that wrote the rule packs wrote these scripts and this page. The defence is that the counting is RAID's code, not ours, and that the predictions were committed first. The page was reviewed adversarially before merging; the reviews are not published.

## Re-run it yourself

See [tools/raid/README.md](../tools/raid/README.md). In short: download `train_none.csv`, draw the sample with `tools/raid/sample.py`, score it with `signsofai-calibrate raid`, count it with `tools/raid/evaluate.py`, attack it with `tools/raid/attack.py`, and write this page with `tools/raid/report.py`. The id fingerprint above says whether you drew the same sample.
